newsitem.title: USA: Florida drenched by Tropical Storm Josephine.
newsitem.headline: Florida drenched by Tropical Storm Josephine.

text.p: More than a dozen tornadoes spun across Florida as Tropical Storm Josephine pushed across the state's northern Gulf coast early on Tuesday with heavy rain and a storm surge that swallowed up coastal roads.
Georgia, South Carolina and much of the U.S. eastern seaboard were expected to feel the effects of the storm later on Tuesday, according to forecasters at the National Hurricane Center.

The Suwannee River, which snakes from southern Georgia into northern Florida, spilled out of its banks by midnight on Monday. The river, made famous by a Stephen Foster song, empties into the Gulf of Mexico.

Although the storm never graduated to hurricane status, Josephine packed a powerful punch with 65 mph (105 km) winds that ripped down coastal power lines in three northern Florida counties and left most of the state soggy and windblown. A tornado watch remained in effect for most of the state until 8 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT) on Tuesday.
At least a dozen tornadoes skipped across northern and central Florida late Monday, with one twister destroying trailers in Edgewater, a small community near Daytona Beach, officials said.
By midnight on Monday, the outer edge of Josephine had pushed ashore in a sparsely populated area between Apalachicola and Cross City, Florida.
Electricity was out in the coastal areas of Taylor, Dixie and Levy counties, emergency officials said.
An emergency shelter at Cross City High School, about 12 miles (20 km) inland, held two dozen evacuees from the coastal villages of Horseshoe Beach and Suwannee.

"My home is still not fixed from the 'storm of the century'," said Wanda Peters. Her Horseshoe Beach home was built on 12-foot (3.5 metre) stilts to protect it from flooding. But that wasn't enough in March 1993, when floods caused by the biggest storm ever to hit that area of Florida picked up her home and flung it on a dune 50 yards (45 metres) away.
"I'm not looking forward to having to hunt for my house again," she said.

The 1993 unnamed "storm of the century" swept through Florida's Gulf Coast with heavy rain, killing about 20 people in flooding. As it moved north, the storm turned into a record blizzard that shut down much of the U.S. eastern seaboard.

Some 10,000 residents of low-lying areas in the three counties were urged to evacuate, but many said they preferred to ride out the storm and its flooding in their own homes. A curfew was in effect until dawn to discourage looting.

Josephine was expected to whip up a storm surge of as much as 9 feet (3 metres), compared to a normal tide of just one to two feet (0.3 to 0.6 metres). The storm surge produced fierce, battering waves that often cause the worst damage associated with hurricanes and tropical storms.

Cedar Key resident Mike Lenver was among the many coastal residents who hurried to protect his boats by moving them away from the shoreline. "When you've got three boats, you have to move fast and just put as much distance from the coast as you can," he said.

Flooding was widespread, as the National Hurricane Center warned that Josephine was bearing rainfall of 5 inches (12.5- cm) or more. Parts of the northeastern Florida city of Jacksonville, far from the expected landfall point, were under as much as 3 feet (1 meter) of water by Monday afternoon.
In towns and barrier islands along a 200 mile (320 km) stretch of the Florida Gulf Coast, residents began preparations as Josephine's threatening winds, rain and flood tides closed in.
Josephine stayed just below hurricane strength, which begins with winds of at least 74 mph (118 kph).

A tropical storm warning was in effect for the Florida Gulf coast from Venice to Apalachicola. And on Florida's Atlantic coast, a tropical storm warning was issued for the coastline stretching from Cape Canaveral to the border of North and South Carolina.
